title: A five percent witness tuning bound removed guaranteed sum-signal gains from fixed decoders in eight worm map models
abstract: We tested whether cells with no assumed signal can serve as noise references for a bilateral neural signal. Eight public C. elegans brain maps supplied chemical synapse site membership in a fixed 162-cell panel. A partial shared-release model held each target variance fixed against independent contact noise. At sharing fraction 0.5, ideal full-panel decoders gave median linear information ratios of 1.017 to 1.049 for sum signals and 1.025 to 1.071 for difference signals. Each map had 6 to 16 sum signals that changed from a pair-only loss to a full-panel gain. We then allowed unknown signal in the other cells. For the same fixed decoders, a bound of five percent of a pair-cell signal component removed the gain guarantee for every sum signal in each map. Median critical bounds were 1.04 to 1.99 percent for sum signals and 1.29 to 2.23 percent for difference signals. This uncertainty test was added after the first output. These are exact linear model calculations, not measured neural noise or information. Unknown tuning, release coupling, synaptic effects and circuit dynamics limit biological use. Code, selected sites, decoder weights, hashes and checks support reproduction.

display.caption: At sharing fraction 0.5, full-panel ideal information gains were small. Small unknown signal in other cells removed most gain guarantees. Points summarize different animals; lines only guide the eye.

citations.reason: Reuses its verified 162-cell panel and bilateral name rule. Its source-pair overlap analysis motivated the distinct full-panel decoding test.
Its site-aware covariance model motivates the comparison. This study pools sources and tests signed bilateral signals with signal uncertainty, rather than nonnegative averaging of one source signal.
